terms.gloss: if that is the case; in that case
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.7.2: id sī ita est
Cic. Att. 6.5.1: quō tē, sī ita est, salvum vēnisse gaudeō
terms.comment: Latin needs no noun for “case”: “if it is so”, and for the other case sīn aliter, if not (Cic. Fam. 11.14.3). Since that is the case, quae cum ita sint (Traupman 95). Traupman also gives eō cāsū, in that case (p. 95); Cicero’s letters say sī ita est.

terms.gloss: a person’s case, the position someone is in
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.112: alius in eādem causā nōn dēbeat
Cic. Att. 11.2.3: quī videntur in eādem causā esse
terms.comment: in eādem causā esse, to be in the same case (Lewis & Short: = condiciō). Also a case at law (see case, at law).
What happens unexpectedly: in such a case, of a crisis (Lewis & Short: “such an emergency”). In grammar, the case of a noun (Varro, Cicero).

evidence: Cic. Lael. 6: sunt ista, Laelī (Lewis & Short s.v. sum)

phrases.latin: in Britanniā nihil esse audiō neque aurī neque argentī. id sī ita est, essedum aliquod capiās suādeō et ad nōs quam prīmum recurrās
phrases.english: I hear there is nothing in Britain, neither gold nor silver. If that’s the case, I suggest you grab a war chariot and race back to us as soon as you can

phrases.latin: id sī ita est, omnia faciliōra; sīn aliter, magnum negōtium
phrases.english: if that is the case, everything is easier; if not, it’s a big job
